abstract: Olfaction provides critical information about airborne chemical cues, yet it remains largely underexplored in embodied AI, with limited prior machine olfaction work focusing primarily on semantic odor perception. We introduce OdorSpaces, a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation. OdorSpaces augments Habitat-Sim with 3D odor transport and dispersion simulated by Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), enabling agents to navigate photorealistic indoor environments using both visual and olfactory observations. The benchmark includes two representative source-seeking scenarios: invisible gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization. We develop an initial multimodal reinforcement learning policy that integrates visual observations and olfactory measurements over time. Experiments show that the policy outperforms a diverse set of baselines, establishing a strong reference for future research on visual-olfactory embodied navigation.

sections.body: The paper argues that olfaction is underexplored in embodied AI, and that prior learning work mostly covers semantic odor perception such as classification. It treats odor as spatial: gas comes from localized sources and spreads with airflow, so an agent must move to find it. OdorSpaces couples Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS) odor fields with Habitat-Sim scenes built from Replica and Matterport3D. The benchmark has two scenarios: an invisible propane gas leak and an early-stage methanol pool fire that produces carbon dioxide. The authors also present an initial policy that combines visual, olfactory and pose-history inputs with recurrent memory, which they report as competitive against baselines.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: OdorSpaces provides a physics-based benchmark for navigating toward odor sources using vision and gas sensing.

sections.body: The related work covers three areas. Machine olfaction has focused on semantic odor perception, such as structure-to-odor relations and odor category recognition, rather than odor as a spatial signal. Odor source localization (OSL) splits into plume finding, plume tracking and source declaration, with gradient-based, bio-inspired, probabilistic and multi-robot methods. These are often tested under simplified plume dynamics, limited scene geometry and single controlled testbeds. Multimodal embodied navigation, especially audio-visual navigation, uses sound as a cue. The paper argues that odor differs because it is a time-varying concentration field shaped by transport, so weak and history-dependent cues require integrating gas measurements over time.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Machine olfaction work mainly addresses semantic odor perception, and source localization methods often use simplified plumes.

sections.body: The task is odor-source seeking. At each step the agent receives visual observations, olfactory measurements and pose history, and picks an action from `move_forward`, `turn_left`, `turn_right` and `stop`. The source is not visible, and the episode has a fixed time budget. Odor fields come from FDS, which solves a low-Mach-number form of the Navier-Stokes equations with large-eddy simulation. Propane is released as a dense gas that settles near the floor. In the methanol pool fire, carbon dioxide rises by buoyancy and serves as a surrogate burning-odor cue. Scenes are 17 Replica and 25 Matterport3D environments, split 9/4/4 and 13/6/6, discretized into a 0.5 m navigation grid. The olfactory sensor is idealized and the fields are precomputed, so real sensor noise and hardware effects are not modeled.
sections.heading: OdorSpaces: A Benchmark for Visual-Olfactory Embodied Navigation
sections.headline: Agents must reach a hidden odor source within a fixed time budget, using precomputed FDS gas fields in Habitat-Sim scenes.

sections.body: Each observation stream has its own encoder: a convolutional encoder for vision and dense encoders for olfaction and pose history. The features are concatenated and passed to a recurrent memory, which feeds a policy head over the discrete actions and a value head. The distance reward gives +0.9 when the agent moves closer to the source and the mean gas concentration rises, +0.5 when it moves closer without that rise, and -0.25 when it moves farther. A stop reward of 15 + 5 times (1 - elapsed time / maximum time) applies at the source, and -2 elsewhere. Training uses a curriculum that raises the initial geodesic distance linearly from 1.5 m to 9.0 m over 30M steps. Episodes start once gas density exceeds a threshold set from 3% of the scene-wise min-max gas density range.
sections.heading: Visual-Olfactory Navigation Policy
sections.headline: A recurrent policy fuses visual, olfactory and pose features and trains with proximal policy optimization.

sections.body: Evaluation uses 10 episodes per scene on held-out validation and test scenes, with three test seeds reported as mean and standard deviation. The primary metric, SPL, is zero unless the agent stops at the source, and otherwise scales the shortest path by the executed path length. Final distance to target is also reported. Baselines are three rule-based searches and a dual-recurrent threshold reinforcement learning method. On Replica propane, the policy scores 65.26±6.59 SPL and 1.48±0.47 m final distance, against 54.50±5.50 for the learned baseline. On Matterport3D propane, the learned baseline scores 65.41±5.15 against 63.82±7.85 for the policy. On Replica methanol fire, the policy scores 24.72±3.69 against 17.58±3.45 for the learned baseline, and rule-based methods score 0.00. Odor alone scores 14.55±3.53, adding vision gives 19.14±2.78, and the full model gives 24.72±3.69.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: The policy has the top mean success-weighted path length in three of four settings; the only exception is Matterport3D propane.

sections.body: The conclusion frames visual-olfactory embodied navigation as a new task and OdorSpaces as its simulation benchmark, with standardized protocols for propane and fire scenarios. The policy is described as competitive against diverse baselines in both scenarios. The stated limitations are precomputed odor fields and idealized olfactory sensing. The benchmark also omits robot-induced airflow, ventilation, wind, and practical sensor placement, noise and latency. It covers source localization after a detection event, not full plume finding. Future work would add dynamic airflow, compact sensor configurations, pre-detection plume finding and broader odor sources, aiming at sim-to-real navigation policies.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The paper frames OdorSpaces as a first benchmark for this task and lists precomputed fields and idealized sensing as limits.

sections.body: The appendix gives FDS settings: 0.2 m cells, 600 s simulations, adiabatic scene boundaries, and output at 4 Hz, with no imposed wind or ventilation. It describes the propane release as a volumetric outflow from the source faces and the methanol pool as a 0.1 m deep pyrolysis pool with four pilot flames. Scene processing covers Replica mesh repair, Matterport3D enclosure, and the 0.5 m grid. The dataset totals 11,442 simulations across both scenarios, with up to approximately 2.5 days per scene. The appendix also explains a propane density correction at the source box, the sensor heights, the temporal windows of 4 and 10 FDS timesteps, and baseline details. It adds ablations on curriculum, reward, temporal, spatial and memory choices, and a test of longer spawn distances.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers FDS settings, scene processing, sensor layout, baseline details, extra ablations, and spawn-distance generalization.
